entries.dfd847d7af475c11daabf5f5d0547b9198acbe26: <div sID="gen11975" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="83" osisID="Ps.83" sID="Ps.83"/> <div eID="gen11975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11976" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11977" type="x-p"/> This psalm is the last of those that go under the name of Asaph. It is penned, as most of those, upon a public account, with reference to the insults of the church's enemies, who sought its ruin. Some think it was penned upon occasion of the threatening descent which was made upon the land of Judah in Jehoshaphat's time by the Moabites and Ammonites, those children of Lot here spoken of (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.8">ver. 8</reference>), who were at the head of the alliance and to whom all the other states here mentioned were auxiliaries. We have the story <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.1">2 Chron. xx. 1</reference>, where it is said, The children of Moab and Ammon, and others besides them, invaded the land. Others think it was penned with reference to all the confederacies of the neighbouring nations against Israel, from first to last. The psalmist here makes an appeal and application, I. To God's knowledge, by a representation of their designs and endeavours to destroy Israel, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.1-Ps.83.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. To God's justice and jealousy, both for his church and for his own honour, by an earnest prayer for the defeat of their attempt, that the church might be preserved, the enemies humbled, and God glorified, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.9-Ps.83.18">ver. 9-18</reference>. This, in the singing of it, we may apply to the enemies of the gospel-church, all anti-christian powers and factions, representing to God their confederacies against Christ and his kingdom, and rejoicing in the hope that all their projects will be baffled and the gates of hell shall not prevail against the church.
entries.8030687856e97c187b9de6c2a80213615a23a70e: <div eID="gen11977" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11976" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Complaints against Enemies.</title> <div sID="gen11978" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Keep not thou silence, O God: hold not thy peace, and be not still, O God. <hi type="super">2</hi> For, lo, thine enemies make a tumult: and they that hate thee have lifted up the head. 3 They have taken crafty counsel against thy people, and consulted against thy hidden ones. <hi type="super">4</hi> They have said, Come, and let us cut them off from <hi type="italic">being</hi> a nation; that the name of Israel may be no more in remembrance. <hi type="super">5</hi> For they have consulted together with one consent: they are confederate against thee: <hi type="super">6</hi> The tabernacles of Edom, and the Ishmaelites; of Moab, and the Hagarenes; <hi type="super">7</hi> Gebal, and Ammon, and Amalek; the Philistines with the inhabitants of Tyre; <hi type="super">8</hi> Assur also is joined with them: they have holpen the children of Lot. Selah. <div eID="gen11978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11979" type="x-p"/> The Israel of God were now in danger, and fear, and great distress, and yet their prayer is called, <hi type="italic">A song or psalm;</hi> for singing psalms is not unseasonable, no, not when the harps are hung upon the willow-trees. <div eID="gen11979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11980" type="x-p"/> I. The psalmist here begs of God to appear on the behalf of his injured threatened people (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Keep not thou silence, O God!</hi> but give judgment for us against those that do us an apparent wrong." Thus Jehoshaphat prayed upon occasion of that invasion (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.11">2 Chron. xx. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">Behold, how they reward us, to come to cast us out of thy possession.</hi> Sometimes God seems to connive at the unjust treatment which is given to his people; he keeps silence, as one that either did not observe it or did not concern himself in it; he holds his peace, as if he would observe an exact neutrality, and let them fight it out; he is still, and gives not the enemies of his people any disturbance or opposition, but seems to sit by <hi type="italic">as a man astonished, or as a mighty man that cannot save.</hi> Then he gives us leave to call upon him, as here, "<hi type="italic">Keep not thou silence, O God!</hi> Lord, speak to us by the prophets for our encouragement against our fears" (as he did in reference to that invasion, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.14-2Chr.20.17">2 Chron. xx. 14</reference>, &c.); "Lord, speak for us by the providence and speak against our enemies; speak deliverance to us and disappointment to them." God's speaking is his acting; for with him saying and doing are the same thing. <div eID="gen11980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11981" type="x-p"/> II. He here gives an account of the grand alliance of the neighbouring nations against Israel, which he begs of God to break, and blast the projects of. Now observe here, <div eID="gen11981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11982" type="x-p"/> 1. Against whom this confederacy is formed; it is against the Israel of God, and so, in effect, against the God of Israel. Thus the psalmist takes care to interest God in their cause, not doubting but that, if it appeared that they were for God, God would make it to appear that he was for them, and then they might set all their enemies at defiance; for whom then could be against them? "Lord," says he, "they are thy enemies, and they hate thee." All wicked people are God's enemies (the <hi type="italic">carnal mind is enmity against God</hi>), but especially wicked persecutors; they hated the religious worshippers of God, because they hated God's holy religion and the worship of him. This was that which made God's people so zealous against them—that they fought against God: <hi type="italic">They are confederate against thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.83.5">v. 5</reference>. Were our interest only concerned, we could the better bear it; but, when God himself is struck at, it is time to cry, Help, Lord. <hi type="italic">Keep not thou silence, O God!</hi> He proves that they are confederate against God, for they are so against the people of God, who are near and dear to him, his son, his first-born, his portion, and the lot of his inheritance; he may truly be said to fight against me that endeavours to destroy my children, to root out my family, and to ruin my estate. "Lord," says the psalmist, "they are thy enemies, for they consult against thy hidden ones." Note, God's people are his hidden ones, hidden, (1.) In respect of secresy. Their life is <hi type="italic">hid with Christ in God;</hi> the <hi type="italic">world knows them not;</hi> if they knew them, they would not hate them as they do. (2.) In respect of safety. God takes them under his special protection, hides them in the hollow of his hand; and yet, in defiance of God and his power and promise to secure his people, they will consult to ruin them and <hi type="italic">cast them down from their excellency</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.62.4">Ps. lxii. 4</reference>), and to make a prey of those whom the <hi type="italic">Lord has set apart for himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Ps. iv. 3</reference>. They resolve to destroy those whom God resolves to preserve. <div eID="gen11982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11983" type="x-p"/> 2. How this confederacy is managed. The devil is at the bottom of it, and therefore it is carried on, (1.) With a great deal of heat and violence: <hi type="italic">Thy enemies make a tumult,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.83.2">v. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">The heathen rage,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1">Ps. ii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">The nations are angry,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.11.18">Rev. xi. 18</reference>. They are noisy in their clamours against the people whom they hope to run down with their loud calumnies. This comes in as a reason why God should not keep silence: "The enemies talk big and talk much; Lord, let them not talk all, but do thou <hi type="italic">speak to them in thy wrath,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.2.5">Ps. ii. 5</reference>. (2.) With a great deal of pride and insolence: <hi type="italic">They have lifted up the head.</hi> In confidence of their success, they are so elevated as if they could over-top the Most High and overpower the Almighty. (3.) With a great deal of art and policy: They have <hi type="italic">taken crafty counsel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.83.3">v. 3</reference>. The subtlety of the old serpent appears in their management, and they contrive by all possible means, though ever so base, ever so bad, to gain their point. They are <hi type="italic">profound to make slaughter</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.2">Hos. v. 2</reference>), as if they could outwit Infinite Wisdom. (4.) With a great deal of unanimity. Whatever separate clashing interest they have among themselves, against the people of God they <hi type="italic">consult with one consent</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.5">v. 5</reference>), nor is <hi type="italic">Satan's kingdom divided against itself.</hi> To push on this unholy war, they lay their heads together, and their horns, and their hearts too. <hi type="italic">Fas est et ab hoste doceri—Even an enemy may instruct.</hi> Do the enemies of the church act with one consent to destroy it? Are the kings of the earth of one mind to give their power and honour to the beast? And shall not the church's friends be unanimous in serving her interests? If Herod and Pilate are made friends, that they may join in crucifying Christ, surely Paul and Barnabas, Paul and Peter, will soon be made friends, that they may join in preaching Christ. <div eID="gen11983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11984" type="x-p"/> 3. What it is that is aimed at in this confederacy. They consult not like the Gibeonites to make a league with Israel, that they might strengthen themselves by such a desirable alliance, which would have been their wisdom. They consult, not only to clip the wings of Israel, to recover their new conquests, and check the progress of their victorious arms, not only to keep the balance even between them and Israel, and to prevent their power from growing exorbitant; this will not serve. It is no less than the utter ruin and extirpation of Israel that they design (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Come, let us cut them off from being a nation,</hi> as they cut off the seven nations of Canaan; let us leave them neither root nor branch, but lay their country so perfectly waste <hi type="italic">that the name of Israel may be no more in remembrance,</hi> no, not in history;" for with them they would destroy their Bibles and burn all their records. Such is the enmity of the serpent's seed against the seed of the woman. It is the secret wish of many wicked men that the church of God might not have a being in the world, that there might be no such thing as religion among mankind. Having banished the sense of it out of their own hearts, they would gladly see the whole earth as well rid of it, all its laws and ordinances abolished, all its restraints and obligations shaken off, and all that preach, profess, or practise it cut off. This they would bring it to if it were in their power; but <hi type="italic">he that sits in heaven shall laugh at them.</hi> <div eID="gen11984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11985" type="x-p"/> 4. Who they are that are drawn into this confederacy. The nations that entered into this alliance are here mentioned (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.6-Ps.83.8">v. 6-8</reference>); the Edomites and Ishmaelites, both descendants from Abraham, lead the van; for apostates from the church have been its most bitter and spiteful enemies, witness Julian. These were allied to Israel in blood and yet in alliance against Israel. There are no bonds of nature so strong but the spirit of persecution has broken through them. <hi type="italic">The brother shall betray the brother to death.</hi> Moab and Ammon were the children of righteous Lot; but, as an incestuous, so a degenerate race. The Philistines were long a thorn in Israel's side, and very vexatious. How the inhabitants of Tyre, who in David's time were Israel's firm allies, come in among their enemies, I know not; but that <hi type="italic">Assur</hi> (that is, the Assyrian) <hi type="italic">also is joined with them</hi> is not strange, or that (as the word is) they were <hi type="italic">an arm to the children of Lot.</hi> See how numerous the enemies of God's church have always been. <hi type="italic">Lord, how are those increased that trouble it!</hi> God's heritage was as a speckled bird; all <hi type="italic">the birds round about were against her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.9">Jer. xii. 9</reference>), which highly magnifies the power of God in preserving to himself a church in the world, in spite of the combined force of earth and hell.
entries.02c1d03fedc153c0a61890783b99b221e2605c36: <div eID="gen11985" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Prophetic Imprecations.</title> <div sID="gen11986" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Do unto them as <hi type="italic">unto</hi> the Midianites; as <hi type="italic">to</hi> Sisera, as <hi type="italic">to</hi> Jabin, at the brook of Kison: <hi type="super">10</hi> <hi type="italic">Which</hi> perished at Endor: they became <hi type="italic">as</hi> dung for the earth. <hi type="super">11</hi> Make their nobles like Oreb, and like Zeeb: yea, all their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna: <hi type="super">12</hi> Who said, Let us take to ourselves the houses of God in possession. 13 O my God, make them like a wheel; as the stubble before the wind. <hi type="super">14</hi> As the fire burneth a wood, and as the flame setteth the mountains on fire; <hi type="super">15</hi> So persecute them with thy tempest, and make them afraid with thy storm. <hi type="super">16</hi> Fill their faces with shame; that they may seek thy name, O <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">17</hi> Let them be confounded and troubled for ever; yea, let them be put to shame, and perish: 18 That <hi type="italic">men</hi> may know that thou, whose name alone <hi type="italic">is</hi> JEHOVAH, <hi type="italic">art</hi> the most high over all the earth. <div eID="gen11986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11987" type="x-p"/> The psalmist here, in the name of the church, prays for the destruction of those confederate forces, and, in God's name, foretels it; for this prayer that it might be so amounts to a prophecy that it shall be so, and this prophecy reaches to all the enemies of the gospel-church; whoever they be that oppose the kingdom of Christ, here they may read their doom. The prayer is, in short, that these enemies, who were confederate against Israel, might be defeated in all their attempts, and that they might prove their own ruin, and so God's Israel might be preserved and perpetuated. Now this is here illustrated, <div eID="gen11987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11988" type="x-p"/> I. By some precedents. Let that be their punishment which has been the fate of others who have formerly set themselves against God's Israel. The defeat and discomfiture of former combinations may be pleaded in prayer to God and improved for the encouragement of our own faith and hope, because God is the same still that ever he was, the same to his people and the same against his and their enemies; with him is no variableness. 1. He prays that their armies might be destroyed as the armies of former enemies had been (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.9-Ps.83.10">v. 9, 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Do to them as to the Midianites;</hi> let them be routed by their own fears, for so the Midianites were, more than by Gideon's 300 men. Do to them as to the army under the command of Sisera (who was general under Jabin king of Canaan) which God discomfited (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.15">Judg. iv. 15</reference>) at the brook Kishon, near to which was Endor. <hi type="italic">They became as dung on the earth;</hi> their dead bodies were thrown like dung laid in heaps, or spread, to fatten the ground; they were trodden to dirt by Barak's small but victorious army; and this was fitly made a precedent here, because Deborah made it so to aftertimes when it was fresh. <reference osisRef="Judg.5.31">Judg. v. 31</reference>, <hi type="italic">So let all thy enemies perish, O Lord!</hi> that is, So they shall perish. 2. He prays that their leaders might be destroyed as they had been formerly. The common people would not have been so mischievous if their princes had not set them on, and therefore they are particularly prayed against, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.11-Ps.83.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. Observe, (1.) What their malice was against the Israel of God. They said, <hi type="italic">Let us take to ourselves the houses of God in possession</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.12">v. 12</reference>), the <hi type="italic">pleasant places</hi> of God (so the word is), by which we may understand the land of Canaan, which was a pleasant land and was Immanuel's land, or the temple, which was indeed God's pleasant place (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.11">Isa. lxiv. 11</reference>), or (as Dr. Hammond suggests) the pleasant pastures, which these Arabians, who traded in cattle, did in a particular manner seek after. The princes and nobles aimed to enrich themselves by this war; and their armies must be made as dung for the earth, to serve their covetousness and their ambition. (2.) What their lot should be. They shall be made <hi type="italic">like Oreb and Zeeb</hi> (two princes of the Midianites, who, when their forces were routed, were taken in their flight by the Ephraimites and slain, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.25">Judg. vii. 25</reference>), and <hi type="italic">like Zeba and Zalmunna,</hi> whom Gideon himself slew, <reference osisRef="Judg.8.21">Judg. viii. 21</reference>. "Let these enemies of ours be made as easy a prey to us as they were to the conquerors then." We may not prescribe to God, but we may pray to God that he will deal with the enemies of his church in our days as he did with those in the days of our fathers. <div eID="gen11988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11989" type="x-p"/> II. He illustrates it by some similitudes, and prays, 1. That God would <hi type="italic">make them like a wheel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.13">v. 13</reference>), that they might be in continual motion, unquiet, unsettled, and giddy in all their counsels and resolves, that they might roll down easily and speedily to their own ruin. Or, as some think, that they might be broken by the judgments of God, as the corn is broken, or beaten out, by the wheel which was then used in threshing. Thus, when a <hi type="italic">wise king scatters the wicked,</hi> he is said to <hi type="italic">bring the wheel over them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.20.26">Prov. xx. 26</reference>. Those that trust in God have their hearts fixed; those that fight against him are unfixed, like a wheel. 2. That they might be chased as <hi type="italic">stubble,</hi> or chaff, <hi type="italic">before the</hi> fierce <hi type="italic">wind.</hi> "The wheel, though it continually turn round, is fixed on its own axis; but let them have no more fixation than the light stubble has, which the wind hurries away, and nobody desires to save it, but is willing it should go," <reference osisRef="Ps.1.4">Ps. i. 4</reference>. Thus shall <hi type="italic">the wicked be driven away in his wickedness, and chased out of the world.</hi> 3. That they might be consumed, as wood by the fire, or as briers and thorns, as fern or furze, upon the mountains, by the flames, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.14">v. 14</reference>. When the stubble is driven by the wind it will rest, at last, under some hedge, in some ditch or other; but he prays that they might not only be driven away as stubble, but burnt up as stubble. And this will be the end of wicked men (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.8">Heb. vi. 8</reference>) and particularly of all the enemies of God's church. The application of these comparisons we have (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">So persecute them with thy tempest,</hi> persecute them to their utter ruin, and make <hi type="italic">them afraid with thy storm.</hi> See how sinners are made miserable; the storm of God's wrath raises terrors in their own hearts, and so they are made completely miserable. God can deal with the proudest and most daring sinner that has bidden defiance to his justice, and can make him afraid as a grasshopper. It is the torment of devils that they tremble. <div eID="gen11989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11990" type="x-p"/> III. He illustrates it by the good consequences of their confusion, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.16-Ps.83.18">v. 16-18</reference>. He prays here that God, having filled their hearts with terror, would thereby fill their faces with shame, that they might be ashamed of their enmity to the people of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Isa. xxvi. 11</reference>), ashamed of their folly in acting both against Omnipotence itself and their own true interest. They did what they could to put God's people to shame, but the shame will at length return upon themselves. Now, 1. The beginning of this shame might be a means of their conversion: "Let them be broken and baffled in their attempts, <hi type="italic">that they may seek thy name, O Lord!</hi> Let them be put to a stand, that they may have both leisure and reason to pause a little, and consider who it is that they are fighting against and what an unequal match they are for him, and may therefore humble and submit themselves and desire conditions of peace. Let them be made to fear thy name, and perhaps that will bring them to seek thy name." Note, That which we should earnestly desire and beg of God for our enemies and persecutors is that God would bring them to repentance, and we should desire their abasement in order to this, no other confusion to them than what may be a step towards their conversion. 2. If it did not prove a means of their conversion, the perfecting of it would redound greatly to the honour of God. If they will not be ashamed and repent, let them be put to shame and perish; if they will not be troubled and turned, which would soon put an end to all their trouble, a happy end, <hi type="italic">let them be troubled for ever,</hi> and never have peace: this will be for God's glory (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.18">v. 18</reference>), that other men may know and own, if they themselves will not, <hi type="italic">that thou, whose name alone is JEHOVAH</hi> (that incommunicable, though not ineffable name) <hi type="italic">art the Most High over all the earth.</hi> God's triumphs over his and his church's enemies will be incontestable proofs, (1.) That he is, according to his name JEHOVAH, a self-existent self-sufficient Being, that has all power and perfection in himself. (2.) That he is the most high God, sovereign Lord of all, above all gods, above all kings, above all that exalt themselves and pretend to be high. (3.) That he is so, not only over the land of Israel, but <hi type="italic">over all the earth,</hi> even those nations of the earth that do not know him or own him; for his kingdom rules over all. These are great and unquestionable truths, but men will hardly be persuaded to know and believe them; therefore the psalmist prays that the destruction of some might be the conviction of others. The final ruin of all God's enemies, in the great day, will be the effectual proof of this, before angels and men, when the everlasting shame and contempt to which sinners shall rise (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Dan. xii. 2</reference>) shall redound to the everlasting honour and praise of that God to whom vengeance belongs.  <chapter eID="Ps.83"/> <div eID="gen11990" type="x-p"/>

The historical occasion is probably that of <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.1">2Ch 20:1</reference>, 2 (compare Psa 47:1-9; 48:1-14). They destroyed one another (Jud 4:6-24; 7:25). Human remains form manure (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.37">2Ki 9:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.22">Jr 9:22</reference>). <div eID="gen9911" type="x-p"/>

The language of the invaders.<div eID="gen9912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">houses--</hi>literally, "residences," enclosures, as for flocks (<reference osisRef="Ps.65.12">Psa 65:12</reference>).<div eID="gen9913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9914" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of God--</hi>as the proprietors of the land (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.11">2Ch 20:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.25">Is 14:25</reference>). <div eID="gen9914" type="x-p"/>

entries.d47ed1cbd57093ed1432de86f4109afcce4b98b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6472"/><div sID="gen9917" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6472"/><hi type="bold">16. that they may seek--</hi>or as <reference osisRef="Ps.83.18">Psa 83:18</reference>, supply "men," since <reference osisRef="Ps.83.17">Psa 83:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.18">18</reference> amplify the sentiment of <reference osisRef="Ps.83.16">Psa 83:16</reference>, expressing more fully the measure of destruction, and the lesson of God's being and perfections (compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.29">2Ch 20:29</reference>) taught to all men. <chapter eID="Ps.83"/>

entries.b976bd6392c1f5fcc633c892867c32388e7b2951: <div eID="gen21286" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21287" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21288" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21288" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21287" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21289" type="x-p"/> The psalmist calls upon God for immediate help against a multitude of confederate enemies who had risen up against Judah, <reference osisRef="Psa.83.1-Psa.83.5">Psa 83:1-5</reference>. He mentions them by name, <reference osisRef="Psa.83.6-Psa.83.8">Psa 83:6-8</reference>; shows how they were to be punished, <reference osisRef="Psa.83.9-Psa.83.17">Psa 83:9-17</reference>; and that this was to be done for the glory of God, <reference osisRef="Psa.83.18">Psa 83:18</reference>. <div eID="gen21289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21290" type="x-p"/> The title, A Song or Psalms of Asaph, contains nothing particular. Among a multitude of conjectures relative to the title and occasion of this Psalm, that which refers it to the confederacy against Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, mentioned 2 Chronicles 20, is the most likely. The following reasons make it probable: 1. The children of Ammon, that is, the Ammonites and Moabites, were the principal movers in the war. 2. The Idumeans came to their assistance, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.22">2Chr 20:22</reference>; with certain Ammonites or Meonians, referred to here in <reference osisRef="Psa.83.8">Psa 83:8</reference>, and in <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.1">2Chr 20:1</reference>. 3. There were also in this confederacy many strangers of Syria, and from beyond the sea, most likely the Dead Sea, which seems to indicate the Assyrians, Hagaranes, and Ishmaelites, designed expressly here, <reference osisRef="Psa.83.7">Psa 83:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.83.8">Psa 83:8</reference>. 4. In that transaction there was a prophet of the race of Asaph, named Jahaziel, who foretold to Jehoshaphat their total overthrow, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.14">2Chr 20:14</reference>, etc., and probably this Jahaziel is the same with Asaph, the author of this Psalm. In the course of the notes we shall see other circumstances relative to the war of the Moabites and Ammonites against Jehoshaphat, which illustrates several particulars in this Psalm. See Calmet. <div eID="gen21290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21291" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21292" type="x-p"/> Keep not thou silence - A strong appeal to God just as the confederacy was discovered. Do not be inactive, do not be neuter. Thy honor and our existence are both at stake.
entries.20bd1748c540ea3eb0df156b19c21bdca97e84aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21293" type="x-p"/> Thine enemies make a tumult - They are not merely the enemies of thy people, but they are the enemies of thyself, thy worship, ordinances, and laws: "They make a tumult," they throng together. <div eID="gen21293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21294" type="x-p"/> They - have lifted up the head - They have made an irruption into the land of Judea, and encamped at En-gedi, by the Dead Sea, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.1">2Chr 20:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.2">2Chr 20:2</reference>.
entries.0d5f0a57a11d6d213aa9c5e0470879cd112a913d: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21295" type="x-p"/> Consulted against thy hidden ones - צפוניך tsephuneycha, Thy hidden things; places; persons. "The hidden things in thy treasures." - Chaldee. "Thy holy ones." - Syriac. "Thy saints." - Vulgate and Septuagint; and so the Ethiopic and Arabic. The people of Israel are probably meant. Or perhaps the temple, the ark, and the treasures of the temple, are intended.
entries.ad1997f32f21013f39f09d9ad3e2258fa66fb220: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21296" type="x-p"/> Let us cut them off - Let us exterminate the whole race, that there may not be a record of them on the face of the earth. And their scheme was well laid: eight or ten different nations united themselves in a firm bond to do this; and they had kept their purpose so secret that the king of Judah does not appear to have heard of it till his territories were actually invaded, and the different bodies of this coalition had assembled at En-gedi. Never was Judah before in greater danger.
entries.d9fb29142f3d8e20e63dfaa1b47ec22d2f39796a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21297" type="x-p"/> They have consulted together with one consent - With a united heart, לב יחדו leb yachdav, Their heart and soul are in the work. <div eID="gen21297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21298" type="x-p"/> They are confederate against thee - "They have made a covenant," ברית יכריתו berith yachrithu, "they have cut the covenant sacrifice." They have slain an animal, divided him in twain, and passed between the pieces of the victim; and have thus bound themselves to accomplish their purpose.
entries.73940c3ce72556dc75862cc0ff1bbf91c5d26e8c: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21299" type="x-p"/> The tabernacles of Edom - The tents of these different people are seen in the grand encampment. Tents are probably mentioned because it seas the custom of some of these people, particularly the lshmaelites, to live a migratory or wandering life; having no fixed habitation, but always abiding in tents. Their posterity remain to the present day, and act and live in the same manner. <div eID="gen21299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21300" type="x-p"/> Hagarenes - These people dwelt on the east of Gilead; and were nearly destroyed in the days of Saul, being totally expelled from their country, <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.10">1Chr 5:10</reference>, but afterwards recovered some strength and consequence; but where they dwelt after their expulsion by the Israelites is not known.
entries.fc6fbddcb8f820d0db1dd6789060d225864f6386: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21301" type="x-p"/> Gebal - The Giblites, who were probably the persons here designed, were a tribe of the ancient inhabitants of the land of Canaan, and are mentioned as unconquered at the death of Joshua, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.5">Jos 13:5</reference>. They are called stone-squarers or Giblites, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.18">1Kgs 5:18</reference>, and were of considerable assistance to Hiram king of Tyre, in preparing timber and stones for the building of the temple. They appear to have been eminent in the days of Ezekiel, who terms them the "ancients of Gebal, and the wise men - thereof," who were ship-builders, <reference osisRef="Eze.27.3">Eze 27:3</reference>. What is now called Gibyle, a place on the Mediterranean Sea, between Tripoli and Sidon, is supposed to be the remains of the city of the Giblites. <div eID="gen21301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21302" type="x-p"/> Ammon and Moab were then descendants of the children of Lot. Their bad origin is sufficiently known. See <reference osisRef="Gen.19.30">Gen 19:30</reference>, etc. Calmet supposes that Ammon is put here for Men or Maon, the Meonians, a people who lived in the neighborhood of the Amalekites and Idumeans. See the notes on <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.1">2Chr 20:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.7">2Chr 26:7</reference>. <div eID="gen21302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21303" type="x-p"/> Amalek - The Amalekites are well known as the ancient and inveterate enemies of the Israelites. They were neighbors to the Idumeans. <div eID="gen21303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21304" type="x-p"/> The Philistines - These were tributaries to Jehoshaphat, <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.11">2Chr 17:11</reference>; but it seems they took advantage of the present times, to join in the great confederacy against him. <div eID="gen21304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21305" type="x-p"/> The inhabitants of Tyre - These probably joined the confederacy in hopes of making conquests, and extending their territory on the main land.
entries.45f469a5201c8207e56db1a4ac599b23afa417aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21306" type="x-p"/> Asser also is joined - The Ammonites might have got those auxiliaries from beyond the Euphrates, against Jehosphaphat, as formerly they were brought against David. See <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.16">2Sam 10:16</reference>. <div eID="gen21306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21307" type="x-p"/> They have holpen the children of Lot - The Ammonites, who appear to have been the chief instigators in this war.
entries.365312f79c86f4fe9433563bebeac294e0eda46f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21308" type="x-p"/> Do unto them as unto the Midianites - Who were utterly defeated by Gideon, <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.21">Jdg 7:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.22">Jdg 7:22</reference>. <div eID="gen21308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21309" type="x-p"/> As to Sisera - Captain of the army of Jabin, king of Canaan, who was totally defeated by Deborah and Barak, near Mount Tabor, by the river Kishon; and himself, after having fled from the battle, slain by Jael, the wife of Heber, the Kenite. See <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.15">Jdg 4:15</reference>, etc.
entries.d02e25db6aa7785293190bb284ebdfa37269f762: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen21309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21310" type="x-p"/> Perished at En-dor - This refers to the defeat of the Midianites by Gideon, who were encamped in the valley of Jezreel, at the foot of Mount Gilboa, and near to Tabor, <reference osisRef="Jdg.6.33">Jdg 6:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.1">Jdg 7:1</reference>, and consequently in the environs of En-dor. There Gideon attacked and defeated them; and, in various places during their flight, they were destroyed, and left to rot upon the earth. <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.22-Jdg.7.25">Jdg 7:22-25</reference>.
entries.7d66883624f0b6dc076a3262c93e34ece542b435: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen21310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21311" type="x-p"/> Lake their nobles like Oreb, and like Zeeb - They were two of the chiefs, or generals, of the Midianites; and were slain in the pursuit of the Midianites, by the men of Ephraim; and their heads brought to Gideon on the other side of JorDaniel <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.24">Jdg 7:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.7.25">Jdg 7:25</reference>. <div eID="gen21311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21312" type="x-p"/> Yea, all their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna - These were kings of Midian, who were encamped at Karkor with fifteen thoussand men, whom Gideon attacked there, and defeated, and took the kings prisoners; and finding that they had killed his own brothers slew them both. See <reference osisRef="Jdg.8.10-Jdg.8.21">Jdg 8:10-21</reference>. Of the Midianites there fell at this time one hundred and twenty thousand men.
entries.2728e66d0605cdc43829e8105eb669fe5c0faad8: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen21312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21313" type="x-p"/> Let us take to ourselves the houses of God in possession - Nearly the words spoken by the confederates when they came to attack Jehoshaphat. They come (says the king in address to God) to cast us out of thy possession which thou hast given us to inherit. See <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.11">2Chr 20:11</reference>.
entries.d7fa77c4bcf7b4325dd1c4d52272a6f43014fa73: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen21313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21314" type="x-p"/> O may God, make them like a wheel - Alluding to the manner of threshing corn in the east. A large broad wheel was rolled over the grain on a threshing-floor, which was generally in the open air; and the grain being thrown up by a shovel against the wind the chaff was thus separated from it, in the place where it was threshed.
entries.3bdaeadd86a8488f4899d7f17293c2b7d8e7d024: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen21314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21315" type="x-p"/> The flame setteth the mountains on fire - This may refer to the burning of the straw and chaff, after the grain was threshed and winnowed. And as their threshing-floors were situated often on the hills or mountains, to take the advantage of the wind, the setting the mountains on fire may refer to the burning of the chaff, etc., in those places. Let them be like stubble driven away by the wind, and burnt by the fire.
entries.77abfb92f968e809aae6a28384ccfff628690cf9: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen21315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21316" type="x-p"/> So persecute them - In this and the two following verses we find several awful execrations; and all this seems to be done in reference to that ancient custom, "pouring execrations on an enemy previously to battle." Of this I have already given specimens in this work; and the reader is particularly requested to refer to the case of Balaam being hired by the king of Moab to curse Israel previously to his intended attack: see the note on <reference osisRef="Num.22.6">Num 22:6</reference>, where the subject is treated at large. <div eID="gen21316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21317" type="x-p"/> This custom prevailed much among the Romans, and the ancient Druids of Britain. In all cases the priests were employed to utter the execrations, as they were supposed to have the greatest influence with the gods, in whose name the curses were uttered.
entries.1983fba59a76fa99e9da345a1f3779e4113bcbbd: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen21317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21318" type="x-p"/> That they may seek thy name - Let them be confounded in all their attempts on Israel; and see, so manifestly, that thou hast done it, that they may invoke thy name, and be converted to thee.
entries.c700b2bb8b8a6aa97b8f8115fd53379888e3ed79: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen21318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21319" type="x-p"/> Let them - perish - That is, in their present attempts. Some have objected to the execrations in this Psalm, without due consideration. None of these execrations refer either to their souls or to their eternal state; but merely to their discomfiture on their present attempts. Suppose the continental powers should join together to subjugate Britain, and destroy the Protestant religion; is there a Christian in the land that would not be justified in meeting them with the same or similar execrations? On the knees of my soul would I offer every one of them to God against such invaders. Selah - A. C.
entries.ce9b4aaa3104f2e5c4bacef29f59a90fd2054c24: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen21319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21320" type="x-p"/> That men may know - That they may acknowledge, and be converted to thee. Here is no malice; all is self-defense.  <chapter eID="Ps.83"/> <div eID="gen21320" type="x-p"/>

entries.84cdf28791e81d6e5f34ecbd90c8a81c8029e035: <div eID="gen9841" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Battle-Cry to God against Allied Peoples</title> <div sID="gen9842" type="x-p"/> The close of this Psalm is in accord with the close of the preceding Psalm. It is the last of the twelve Psalms of Asaph of the Psalter. The poet supplicates help against the many nations which have allied themselves with the descendants of Lot, i.e., Moab and Ammon, to entirely root out Israel as a nation. Those who are fond of Maccabaean Psalms (Hitzig and Olshausen), after the precedent of van Til and von Bengel, find the circumstances of the time of the Psalm in 1 Macc. 5, and Grimm is also inclined to regard this as correct; and in point of fact the deadly hostility of the ἔθνη κυκλόθεν which we there see breaking forth on all sides,<note placement="foot">Concerning the υίοὶ Βαΐάν (<hi type="italic">Benı̂ Baijân</hi>), 1 Macc. 5:4, the difficulty respecting which is to the present time unsolved, vid., Wetzstein’s Excursus II, pp. 559f..</note> as it were at a given signal, against the Jewish people, who have become again independent, and after the dedication of the Temple doubly self-conscious, is far better suited to explain the Psalm than the hostile efforts of Sanballat, Tobiah, and others to hinder the rebuilding of Jerusalem, in the time of Nehemiah (Vaihinger, Ewald, and Dillmann). There is, however, still another incident beside that recorded in 1 Macc. 5 to which the Psalm may be referred, viz., the confederation of the nations for the extinction of Judah in the time of Jehoshaphat (2 Chr. 20), and, as it seems to us, with comparatively speaking less constraint. For the Psalm speaks of a real league, whilst in 1 Macc. 5 the several nations made the attack without being allied and not jointly; then, as the Psalm assumes in <reference osisRef="Ps.83.9">Psa 83:9</reference>, the sons of Lot, i.e., the Moabites and Ammonites, actually were at the head at that time, whilst in 1 Macc. 5 the sons of Esau occupy the most prominent place; and thirdly, at that time, in the time of Jehoshaphat, as is recorded, an Asaphite, viz., Jahaziël, did actually interpose in the course of events, a circumstance which coincides remarkably with the לאסף. The league of that period consisted, according to <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.1">2Ch 20:1</reference>, of Moabites, Ammonites, and a part of the מעוּנים (as it is to be read after the lxx). But <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.2">2Ch 20:2</reference> (where without any doubt מאדם is to be read instead of מארם) adds the Edomites to their number, for it is expressly stated further on (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.10">2Ch 20:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.22">2Ch 20:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.23">2Ch 20:23</reference>) that the inhabitants of Mount Seïr were with them. Also, supposing of course that the “Ishmaelites” and “Hagarenes” of the Psalm may be regarded as an unfolding of the מעונים, which is confirmed by Josephus, <hi type="italic">Antiq</hi>. ix. 1. 2; and that Gebäl is to be understood by the Mount Seïr of the chronicler, which is confirmed by the Arab. <hi type="italic">jibâl</hi> still in use at the present day, there always remains a difficulty in the fact that the Psalm also names <hi type="italic">Amalek , Philistia , Tyre</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Asshur</hi>, of which we find no mention there in the reign of Jehoshaphat. But these difficulties are counter-balanced by others that beset the reference to 1 Macc. 5, viz., that in the time of the Seleucidae the Amalekites no longer existed, and consequently, as might be expected, are not mentioned at all in 1 Macc. 5; further, that there the Moabites, too, are no longer spoken of, although some formerly Moabitish cities of Gileaditis are mentioned; and thirdly, that אשׁור = Syria (a certainly possible usage of the word) appears in a subordinate position, whereas it was, however, the dominant power. On the other hand, the mention of Amalek is intelligible in connection with the reference to 2 Chr. 20, and the absence of its express mention in the chronicler does not make itself particularly felt in consideration of Gen 36:12. Philistia, Tyre, and Asshur, however, stand at the end in the Psalm, and might also even be mentioned with the others if they rendered aid to the confederates of the south-east without taking part with them in the campaign, as being a succour to the actual leaders of the enterprise, the sons of Lot. We therefore agree with the reference of Psalms 83 (as also of <reference osisRef="Ps.48.1-Ps.48.14">Psa 48:1-14</reference>) to the alliance of the neighbouring nations against Judah in the reign of Jehoshaphat, which has been already recognised by Kimchi and allowed by Keil, Hengstenberg, and Movers.
entries.317d10a013ede0c5ac3a0c2fe4624129ef487cc2: <reference osisRef="Ps.83.1-Ps.83.4">Psa 83:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen9842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9843" type="x-p"/> The poet prays, may God not remain an inactive looker-on in connection with the danger of destruction that threatens His people. דּמי (with which יהי is to be supplied) is the opposite of alertness; חרשׁ the opposite of speaking (in connection with which it is assumed that God’s word is at the same time deed); שׁקט the opposite of being agitated and activity. The energetic future <hi type="italic">jehemajûn</hi> gives outward emphasis to the confirmation of the petition, and the fact that Israel’s foes are the foes of God gives inward emphasis to it. On נשׂא ראשׁ, cf. Psa 110:7. סוד is here a secret agreement; and יערימוּ, elsewhere to deal craftily, here signifies to craftily plot, devise, bring a thing about. צפוּניך is to be understood according to <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference>; Psa 31:21. The <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. התיעץ alternates here with the more ancient <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.6">Psa 83:6</reference>). The design of the enemies in this instance has reference to the total extirpation of Israel, of the separatist-people who exclude themselves from the life of the world and condemn it. מגּוי, from being a people = so that it may no longer be a people or nation, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.7.8">Isa 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1">Isa 17:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.2">Isa 25:2</reference>; Jer 48:42. In the borrowed passage, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.2">Jer 48:2</reference>, by an interchange of a letter it is נכריתנּה. This Asaph Psalm is to be discerned in not a few passages of the prophets; cf. Isa 62:6. with <reference osisRef="Ps.83.2">Psa 83:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12">Isa 17:12</reference> with Psa 83:3.
entries.12b9305a3094ea05200ddaac31c61321e156e8bb: <reference osisRef="Ps.83.5-Ps.83.8">Psa 83:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen9843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9844" type="x-p"/> Instead of לב אחד,    <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.38">1Ch 12:38</reference>, it is <hi type="italic">deliberant corde unâ</hi>, inasmuch as יחדּו on the one hand gives intensity to the reciprocal signification of the verb, and on the other lends the adjectival notion to לב. Of the confederate peoples the chronicler (2 Chr. 20) mentions the Moabites, the Ammonites, the inhabitants of Mount Seïr, and the Me(unim, instead of which Josephus, <hi type="italic">Antiq</hi>. ix. 1. 2, says: a great body of Arabians. This crowd of peoples comes from the other side of the Dead Sea, מאדם (as it is to be read in <reference osisRef="Ps.83.2">Psa 83:2</reference> in the chronicler instead of מארם, cf. on <reference osisRef="Ps.60.2">Psa 60:2</reference>); the territory of Edom, which is mentioned first by the poet, was therefore the rendezvous. The tents of Edom and of the Ishmaelites are (cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">ahl</hi>, people) the people themselves who live in tents. Moreover, too, the poet ranges the hostile nations according to their geographical position. The seven first named from Edom to Amalek, which still existed at the time of the psalmist (for the final destruction of the Amalekites by the Simeonites, 1Ch 4:42., falls at an indeterminate period prior to the Exile), are those out of the regions east and south-east of the Dead Sea. According to <reference osisRef="Gen.25.18">Gen 25:18</reference>, the Ishmaelites had spread from Higâz through the peninsula of Sinai beyond the eastern and southern deserts as far up as the countries under the dominion of Assyria. The Hagarenes dwelt in tents from the Persian Gulf as far as the east of Gilead (<reference osisRef="1Chr.5.10">1Ch 5:10</reference>) towards the Euphrates. גּבל, Arab. <hi type="italic">jbâl</hi>, is the name of the people inhabiting the mountains situated in the south of the Dead Sea, that is to say, the northern Seïritish mountains. Both Gebâl and also, as it appears, the Amalek intended here according to <reference osisRef="Gen.36.12">Gen 36:12</reference> (cf. Josephus, <hi type="italic">Antiq</hi>. ii. 1. 2: Ἀμαληκῖτις, a part of Idumaea), belong to the wide circuit of <hi type="italic">Edom</hi>. Then follow the Philistines and Phoenicians, the two nations of the coast of the Mediterranean, which also appear in <reference osisRef="Amos.1.1-Amos.1.15">Amo 1:1-15</reference> (cf. Joel 3) as making common cause with the Edomites against Israel. Finally Asshur, the nation of the distant north-east, here not as yet appearing as a principal power, but strengthening (vid., concerning זרוע, an arm = assistance, succour, Gesenius, <hi type="italic">Thesaurus</hi>, p. 433 <hi type="italic">b</hi>) the sons of Lot, i.e., the Moabites and Ammonites, with whom the enterprise started, and forming a powerful reserve for them. The music bursts forth angrily at the close of this enumeration, and imprecations discharge themselves in the following strophe.
entries.896276a4ad5402316993d27f8a4696dc397dbd3b: <reference osisRef="Ps.83.9-Ps.83.12">Psa 83:9-12</reference> <div eID="gen9844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9845" type="x-p"/> With כּמדין reference is made to Gideon’s victory over the Midianites, which belongs to the most glorious recollections of Israel, and to which in other instances, too, national hopes are attached, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Isa 9:3</reference> [4], <reference osisRef="Isa.10.26">Isa 10:26</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Hab.3.7">Hab 3:7</reference>; and with the asyndeton כּסיסרא כיבין (כּסיסרא, as Norzi states, who does not rightly understand the placing of the <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>) to the victory of Barak and Deborah over Sisera and the Canaanitish king Jabin, whose general he was. The <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of בּנחל is like the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of בּדּרך in <reference osisRef="Ps.110.7">Psa 110:7</reference> : according to Jdg 5:21 the Kishon carried away the corpses of the slain army. <hi type="italic">‛Endôr</hi>, near Tabor, and therefore situated not far distant from Taanach and Megiddo (Jdg 5:19), belonged to the battle-field. אדמה, starting from the radical notion of that which flatly covers anything, which lies in דם, signifying the covering of earth lying flat over the globe, therefore <hi type="italic">humus</hi> (like ארץ, <hi type="italic">terra</hi>, and תבל, <hi type="italic">tellus</hi>), is here (cf. 2Ki 9:37) in accord with דּמן (from דמן), which is in substance akin to it. In <reference osisRef="Ps.83.12">Psa 83:12</reference> we have a retrospective glance at Gideon’s victory. <hi type="italic">‛Oreb</hi> and <hi type="italic">Zeēb</hi> were שׂרים of the Midianites, Jdg 7:25; <hi type="italic">Zebach</hi> and <hi type="italic">Tsalmunna‛</hi>, their kings, Jdg 8:5.<note placement="foot">The Syriac Hexapla has (Hos 10:14) צלמנע instead of שׁלמן, a substitution which is accepted by Geiger, <hi type="italic">Deutsch. Morgenländ. Zeitschr</hi>. 1862, S. 729f. Concerning the signification of the above names of Midianitish princes, vid., Nöldeke, <hi type="italic">Ueber die Amalekiter</hi>, S. 9.</note> <div eID="gen9845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9846" type="x-p"/> The pronoun precedes the word itself in שׁיתמו, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.2.6">Exo 2:6</reference>; the heaped-up suffixes <hi type="italic">ēmo</hi>(<hi type="italic">êmo</hi>)give to the imprecation a rhythm and sound as of rolling thunder. Concerning נסיך, vid., on Psa 2:6. So far as the matter is concerned, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.11">2Ch 20:11</reference> harmonizes with Psa 83:13. Canaan, the land which is God’s and which He has given to His people, is called נאות אלהים (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.74.20">Psa 74:20</reference>).
entries.76110070841ee51aa76a278621bd39bfea68a8ea: <reference osisRef="Ps.83.13-Ps.83.16">Psa 83:13-16</reference> <div eID="gen9846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9847" type="x-p"/> With the אלהי, which constrains God in faith, the “thundering down” begins afresh. גּלגּל signifies a wheel and a whirling motion, such as usually arises when the wind changes suddenly, then also whatever is driven about in the whirling, Isa 17:13.<note placement="foot">Saadia, who renders the גּלגּל in <reference osisRef="Ps.77.19">Psa 77:19</reference> as an astronomical expression with Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - frk</hi>, the sphere of the heavens, here has professedly Arab. <hi type="italic">kâlgrâblt</hi>, which would be a plural from expanded out of Arab. <hi type="italic">grâbı̂l</hi>, “sieves” or “tambourines;” it is, however, to be read, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.17.13">Isa 17:13</reference>, <hi type="italic">Codex Oxon</hi>., Arab. <hi type="italic">kâlgirbâlt</hi>. The verb Arab. <hi type="italic">garbala</hi>, “to sift,” is transferred to the wind, e.g., in <hi type="italic">Mutanabbi</hi> (edited with Wahidi’s commentary by Dieterici), p. 29, l. 5 and 6: “it is as though the dust of this region, when the winds chase one another therein, were sifted,” Arab. <hi type="italic">mugarbalu</hi> (i.e., caught up and whirled round); and with other notional and constructional applications in <hi type="italic">Makkarı̂</hi>, i. p. 102, l. 18: “it is as though its soil had been cleansed from dust by sifting,” Arab. <hi type="italic">gurbilat</hi> (i.e., the dust thereof swept away by a whirlwind). Accordingly Arab. <hi type="italic">girbâlat</hi> signifies first, as a <hi type="italic">nom. vicis</hi>, a whirling about (of dust by the wind), then in a concrete sense a whirlwind, as Saadia uses it, inasmuch as he makes use of it twice for גּלגּל. So Fleischer in opposition to Ewald, who renders “like the sweepings or rubbish.”</note> קשׁ (from קשׁשׁ, Arab. <hi type="italic">qšš , aridum esse</hi>) is the cry corn-talks, whether as left standing or, as in this instance, as straw upon the threshing-floor or upon the field. Like a fire that spreads rapidly, laying hold of everything, which burns up the forest and singes off the wooded mountain so that only a bare cone is left standing, so is God to drive them before Him in the raging tempest of His wrath and take them unawares. The figure in <reference osisRef="Ps.83.15">Psa 83:15</reference> is fully worked up by Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.16-Isa.10.19">Isa 10:16-19</reference>; לחט as in Deu 32:22. In the apodosis, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.16">Psa 83:16</reference>, the figure is changed into a kindred one: wrath is a glowing heat (חרון) and a breath (נשׁמה, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa 30:33</reference>) at the same time. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.83.17">Psa 83:17</reference></hi> it becomes clear what is the final purpose towards which this language of cursing tends: to the end that all, whether willingly or reluctantly, may give the glory to the God of revelation. Directed towards this end the earnest prayer is repeated once more in the tetrastichic closing strain.
entries.89cdb3f9b5038cc7557744166444f691c1c38f6f: <reference osisRef="Ps.83.17-Ps.83.18">Psa 83:17-18</reference> <div eID="gen9847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9848" type="x-p"/> The aim of the wish is that they in the midst of their downfall may lay hold upon the mercy of Jahve as their only deliverance: first they must come to nought, and only by giving Jahve the glory will they not be utterly destroyed. Side by side with אתּה, v. 19 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, is placed שׁמך as a second subject (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.44.3">Psa 44:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.11">Psa 69:11</reference>). In view of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.83.17">Psa 83:17</reference></hi> וידעוּ (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.59.14">Psa 59:14</reference>) has not merely the sense of perceiving so far as the justice of the punishment is concerned; the knowledge which is unto salvation is not excluded. The end of the matter which the poet wishes to see brought about is this, that Jahve, that the God of revelation (שׁמך), may become the All-exalted One in the consciousness of the nations.  <chapter eID="Ps.83"/> <div eID="gen9848" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 83
The prophet implores the divine aid against the enemies of the Church, and, as an argument for obtaining this the more easily, he enumerates the many nations which had conspired together for the express purpose of exterminating the people of Israel, and thereby extinguishing the very name of the Church of God. To stir up himself and others to greater earnestness and confidence in prayer, he shows, by many examples, how mightily God had been wont to succor his servants.
A Song or Psalm of Asaph.
Psalm 83:1-4
1. O God! keep not silence with thyself; hold not thy peace, and be not still, O God! 2. For, behold! Thy enemies are tumultuous: and those who hate thee have lifted up the head. 3. They have formed a crafty design against thy people, and have consulted against thy hidden ones. 4. They have said, Come and let us cut them off from being a nation; and let the name of Israel be no more remembered.
 
1 O God! hold not thy peace. It is very generally agreed among commentators, that this psalm was composed during the reign of king Jehoshaphat; and in this opinion I readily concur. That godly king, as is well known, had to engage in dreadful wars against multiplied hosts of enemies. Although the Ammonites and Moabites were the originators of the principal war in which he was engaged, yet they mustered forces not only from Syria, but also from distant countries, and the troops thus brought together well nigh overwhelmed Judea with their multitude. It would then appear, from the long list of enemies, here enumerated, who had conspired together to destroy the people of God, that the conjecture is well-founded which refers the composition of this psalm to that occasion;
Compare the 6th, 7th, and 8th verses of the psalm with 2 Chronicles 20:1, 10, 22; and the 12th verse of the psalm with the 11th verse of that chapter.
and sacred history informs us, that one of the Levites, under the influence of the Spirit of prophecy, gave the king assurance of victory,
The name of this Levite was Jahaziel, and he is expressly said to be a prophet of the race of Asaph, 2 Chronicles 20:14. It is not unlikely that he is the same with Asaph, the author of this psalm.
and that the Levites sang before the Lord. In the midst of so great dangers, the whole nation, as well as the holy king, must have been involved in the deepest distress; and, accordingly, we have here a prayer full of earnestness and solicitude. These feelings prompted the repetition of the words which occur in the very opening of the psalm, Hold not thy peace, Keep not silence, be not still By this, the faithful would intimate, that if God intended to succor them, it behoved him to make haste, else the opportunity for doing so would be lost. It is unquestionably our duty to wait patiently when God at any time delays his help; but, in condescension to our infirmity, he permits us to supplicate him to make haste. What I have rendered, keep not silence with thyself, is literally keep not silence to thyself, which some translate by the paraphrase, Hold not thy peace in thy own cause, — an exposition which is too refined to be more particularly noticed. This form of expression is equivalent to saying, Hold not thyself in. Perhaps the particle is here superfluous, as it is in many other places.

                  <ns0:head>PSAL. LXXXIII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:head>The ARGUMENT.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p>The occasion of the <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> is manifest from the body of it; and it seems to have been a dangerous at<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tempt, and conspiracy of divers neighouring Nations against <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Judah.</ns0:hi> Probably it was that which is mentioned <ns0:hi>2 Chron. 20.</ns0:hi> Wherein all the people here mentioned might be ingaged, though all of them be not there expressed; this being usual in the sacred Historians for the latter to record some passa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ges which the former omitted. Or it may belong to some other History. Or it may have a more gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral respect unto the several Enterprizes and Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />binations of all all these people against them, some at one time, and some at another.</ns0:p>

                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> Asaph.</ns0:note> of Asaph.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 KEep not thou silence <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Plead for us, not by words, but by thine Actions.</ns0:note>, O God: hold not thy peace <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>be not deaf,</ns0:hi> to our prayers, and to the blasphemies of thine and our Enemies.</ns0:note>, and be not still <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Unactive and unconcern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed for us.</ns0:note>, O God.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 For lo, thine enemies <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">They are not onely enemies to us thy people, but also to thy Will, and Name, and Glory.</ns0:note> make a tumult <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>make a tumultuous noise</ns0:hi> both with their tongues reproaching thee, and threat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning us, and with their Arms.</ns0:note>: and they that hate thee, have lift up the head <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Are grown potent, and insolent and scornful.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 They have taken crafty counsel against thy people and consulted against thy hidden ones <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Thy People of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> as it is explained in the foregoing words, and in the next Verse; who are called God's <ns0:hi>hidden</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>secret ones,</ns0:hi> to intimate the singular care and respect which God hath to them, as to his <ns0:hi>peculiar treasure,</ns0:hi> as they are called <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19. 5. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 135. 4. whom he will hide and preserve in the secret of his presence, and under the sha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dow of his wings; and withal to note their folly in seeking the destruction of those whom God was ingaged and resolved to protect.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 They have said, Come, and let us cut them off from <ns0:hi>being</ns0:hi> a nation: that the name of Israel may be no more in remembrance <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Whereby they shewed both their implacable rage and malice, and their great assurance of success.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 For they have consulted together with one <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> heart.</ns0:note> consent: they are confederate against thee <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">They have laid aside all their private quarrels and ani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mosites, and agreed together against thee.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 The tabernacles <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Put for the People dwelling in them, as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 12. 6. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 14. 11. <ns0:hi>Hab.</ns0:hi> 3. 7.</ns0:note> of Edom <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Called <ns0:hi>the children of Seir,</ns0:hi> 2 Chron. 20.</ns0:note>, and the Ishmaelites <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Some of the posterity of <ns0:hi>Ishmael,</ns0:hi> called by their Father's name, as others of them are supposed by divers to be called <ns0:hi>Hagarens</ns0:hi> from their Grandmother <ns0:hi>Hagar.</ns0:hi> See 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 5. 10, 20.</ns0:note> of Moab, and the Hagarenes.</ns0:p>

An <ns0:hi>Arabian</ns0:hi> people so called by ancient Writers dwelling in the Southern Border of <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> where most of the people here mentioned had their abode. Yet some of these were in the Northern p<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                  <ns0:p n="8">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:481" />8 Assur also is joyned with them <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">In their counsels, and possibly with some of their Forces though not so openly and powerfully, as afterwards.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb <ns0:hi>They have been an arm to the chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren of</ns0:hi> Lot.</ns0:note> they have holpen the children of Lot <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">

                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Make their nobles like <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Judg. 7. 25.</ns0:note> Oreb, and like Zeeb: yea, all their princes as <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Judg. 8. 12, 21.</ns0:note> Zebah, and as Zalmunna:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 Who said let us take to our selves the houses of God <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The Houses and Lands of the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> which their God, as they pretend, gave them in <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> to which they have no rightful Title. So they seem to call them <ns0:hi>houses of God,</ns0:hi> by way of irony and Derision.</ns0:note> in possession:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 O my God, make them like a wheel <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Whereas they promise to themselves a sure and firm pos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />session in our Land, let them be like <ns0:hi>a wheel,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>a round ball,</ns0:hi> which being once tumbled down from the top of an hill, runs down with great force and swiftness, and stays not till it comes to the bottom, and there also is very unstable, and soon removed.</ns0:note>: as the Stubble before the wind.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 As the fire burneth the wood, and as the flame setteth the mountains <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Understand by a Metonymy the Woods or Forests upon the Mountains, which in those hot Countries, when they had once taken fire, either by lightning, or by the design of men, or by any accident, did burn with great speed and ir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />resistible violence.</ns0:note> on fire;</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="16">16 Fill their faces with shame: that they may seek thy name <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">That being disappointed of their hopes, and discerning the impotency of their Idols they may own and worship thee as the onely true God.</ns0:note>, O LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 Let them be confounded and troubled for ever: yea, Let them be put to shame, and pe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rish <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">But those of them that will not humble themselves before thee, let them be utterly destroyed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 That <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> may know <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>that they may know,</ns0:hi> to wit, by costly experience, e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven by their own ruine, what they would know by informa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion for their own good. ‖ The most high God, and the God ‖ not onely of his People <ns0:hi>Irael,</ns0:hi> as the Heathen fancied, and as their Gods were confined to their particular and several Territories, but the God and Governor of all the Nations and parts of the earth.</ns0:note>, that thou whose name alone <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> JEHOVAH, <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> the most high over all the earth.</ns0:p>
